scenes.heading: Experiments and relative frequency
scenes.sub: When you can't work it out, try it and count
scenes.say: How likely is a drawing pin to land point up? You can't work that out just by thinking. You have to try it, lots of times, and count. Let's see how.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: 10 shots tell you a little; 200 shots show a player's real skill
scenes.science: More trials give a better estimate of the true probability
scenes.breaks: A shooter improves with practice, but a coin or die never learns. Its true probability stays the same.
scenes.say: If a friend shoots ten hoops and gets seven, you've got a rough idea of their skill. But if you watch two hundred shots, you can really trust the result. Probability experiments work the same way. More trials, better estimate. The difference is, a coin never gets better with practice.

scenes.heading: Relative frequency
scenes.say: Relative frequency is the number of times the event happened, divided by the total number of trials. It's also called experimental probability.

scenes.heading: Theory vs experiment
scenes.say: Theoretical probability is worked out by thinking. A fair coin gives one half. Relative frequency comes from actually doing it. Twenty-eight heads in fifty tosses gives zero point five six. Close, but not exact. With more trials, it usually gets closer to the theory.
scenes.caption: Theoretical probability is worked out by thinking. A fair coin gives 1/2. Relative frequency comes from actually doing it. 28 heads in 50 tosses gives 0.56. Close, but not exact. With more trials, it usually gets closer to the theory.

scenes.heading: More trials, better estimate
scenes.say: Watch what happens as we keep tossing. After ten tosses the relative frequency of heads is zero point seven. By five hundred tosses it has settled right next to the dashed line at one half.
scenes.caption: Watch what happens as we keep tossing. After 10 tosses the relative frequency of heads is 0.7. By 500 tosses it has settled right next to the dashed line at ½.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: A drawing pin lands point up 130 times in 200 drops. Predict for 1000 drops.
scenes.say: A drawing pin lands point up one hundred and thirty times in two hundred drops. The relative frequency is zero point six five. For a thousand drops, multiply: zero point six five times one thousand gives about six hundred and fifty point up, and about three hundred and fifty point down.
scenes.caption: A drawing pin lands point up 130 times in 200 drops. The relative frequency is 0.65. For 1000 drops, multiply: 0.65 × 1000 gives about 650 point up, and about 350 point down.

scenes.heading: 60 rolls of a die
scenes.say: Here are sixty rolls of a die. We expect about ten of each number, shown by the dashed line. The real bars wobble above and below it. That's chance at work.

scenes.heading: Watch out
points: Expected is a best guess, not a promise
Coins and dice have no memory
Judge fairness only after many trials
scenes.say: A few warnings. The expected number is a best guess, not a promise. Coins and dice have no memory, so after five tails, heads is not due. And only call something unfair after a lot of trials.

Quick recap. Relative frequency is times it happened over trials. More trials give a better estimate. Expected number is probability times trials. And dice have no memory. Now try the practice questions!
